rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper buyer-side story in "Airtable's agents can now update your records and draft your emails. It has not said how often they get it wrong." That turns a missing fact into a legitimate enterprise IT angle instead of pretending the launch automatically redraws the market. A has useful bones, but "Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is a competitive-map claim wearing shoes too big for the supplied facts.
gaps_in_A: "Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" overstates the competitive consequence without any named rivals, buyer comparisons, or market-share facts in the update.
"The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" is too sweeping for one company announcement; it needs outside proof before it earns that category claim.
"all-in product pivot" is hotter than the fact set. The update says repositioning and agent launch, not that Airtable has staked the whole company on this move.
It misses the strongest enterprise-buyer angle: agents can update company records while reliability data is undisclosed.
gaps_in_B: "drops the \"spreadsheet-database\" pitch" and "publicly abandoning that identity" are stronger than the facts; the update says shifting messaging, not formally killing the old identity.

"Who is on record? None of the three angles survives contact with a reporter without a named executive." Too absolute. The governance angle could survive with product docs, admin sourcing, and customer proof.
"Airtable takes on the incumbents in the agent-platform race" may be over-refused. A careful competitive-set angle can exist if framed as a question and backed by analyst or buyer proof.
